props.title: The Happiest Millionaire
props.initialSlug: Eccentric millionaire disrupts family with wild antics

sections.content: **The Happiest Millionaire** (1967) represents Disney's last live-action musical personally overseen by Walt Disney before his death. This lavish production stars Fred MacMurray as eccentric millionaire Anthony J. Drexel Biddle, bringing the same fatherly charm he showed in **The Absent-Minded Professor** (1961). The film follows Disney's successful formula established in **Mary Poppins** (1964), combining period setting, family dynamics, and Sherman Brothers songs, though it never reached the same cultural impact. Like **Thoroughly Modern Millie** (1967) from the same year, it captures the transitional period of late 1960s Hollywood musicals before the genre's decline.

sections.content: The film's production values showcase the pinnacle of Disney's 1960s live-action ambitions. The costume design by Bill Thomas, who also worked on **Babes in Toyland** (1961) and **The Gnome-Mobile** (1967), captures the Edwardian era's opulence. Tommy Steele brings Broadway energy similar to his stage work, though the film's lengthy 164-minute runtime (later cut to 144 minutes) reflects the era's tendency toward roadshow-style presentations like **Doctor Dolittle** (1967) and **Star!** (1968).

Based on a true story and earlier stage adaptation, the film follows the real-life Biddle family, with themes of tradition versus progress that echo through other period Disney films like **Summer Magic** (1963) and **Those Calloways** (1965). The Sherman Brothers' score includes memorable numbers like "Fortuosity" and "Let's Have a Drink on It," though they lack the instant recognition of their work in **The Jungle Book** (1967) from the same year. sections.content: **The Happiest Millionaire** (1967) marks the end of an era for Disney live-action musicals that began with **Summer Magic** (1963) and peaked with **Mary Poppins** (1964). The changing cultural landscape of the late 1960s made such wholesome family entertainments seem increasingly out of touch, as evidenced by other struggling musicals like **Doctor Dolittle** (1967) and **Chitty Chitty Bang Bang** (1968). The studio wouldn't attempt another live-action musical on this scale until **Bedknobs and Broomsticks** (1971).
